lesson.title: The Cell's Internal Scaffolding: An Introduction to the Cytoskeleton
lesson.summary: The cytoskeleton is a dynamic network of protein filaments that gives eukaryotic cells their shape, anchors their organelles, and powers movement both within the cell and of the cell itself.
lesson.body:
It is tempting to picture the inside of a eukaryotic cell as a loose bag of fluid with organelles drifting freely inside it, but that picture is misleading. Running throughout the cytoplasm is the cytoskeleton, a dynamic, interconnected network of protein filaments that gives the cell its shape, holds organelles in relatively fixed positions, and provides the tracks and motors needed for movement, both movement of materials within the cell and movement of the cell as a whole. Far from being a passive scaffold, the cytoskeleton is constantly being built, taken apart, and rebuilt in response to what the cell needs to do at any given moment.

The cytoskeleton is made of three main types of protein filaments, each with a distinct structure and role. Microfilaments, built from the protein actin, are the thinnest of the three and are especially important for cell shape, muscle contraction, and cell movement. Microtubules, built from the protein tubulin, are the thickest of the three and form hollow tube-like structures that serve as tracks for transporting organelles and vesicles, and that also build the mitotic spindle used to separate chromosomes during cell division. A third type, intermediate filaments, sits in between the other two in thickness and is generally more stable and less dynamic, providing durable mechanical strength, for example the keratin filaments that reinforce skin cells. Because microfilaments and microtubules are covered as their own topics next, this chapter focuses on what unites all three systems as a coordinated whole.

One of the cytoskeleton's most fundamental jobs is simply giving a cell its shape. Without internal structural support, a cell bounded only by its flexible plasma membrane would have no consistent form, but the cytoskeleton's filaments, working together, allow cells to take on wildly different shapes suited to their function, from the long, thin processes of a neuron to the flattened, elongated form of a muscle cell. The cytoskeleton also anchors organelles in relatively stable positions, preventing them from drifting randomly through the cytosol and helping keep processes like the rough ER to Golgi apparatus secretory pathway spatially organized.

The cytoskeleton is equally essential for movement. Motor proteins, including kinesin, dynein, and myosin, physically walk along microtubule or microfilament tracks, carrying vesicles, organelles, and other cargo to specific destinations within the cell, powered by the energy released from ATP. On a larger scale, coordinated assembly and disassembly of microfilaments allows some cells to crawl by extending and retracting parts of their membrane, and microtubules organized into specialized bundles form the core of cilia and flagella, the whip-like or hair-like structures some cells use for locomotion or for moving fluid across their surface.

Because eukaryotic cells are large and internally compartmentalized, with membrane-bound organelles like the nucleus, ER, and mitochondria distributed throughout the cytoplasm, they face an organizational challenge that simpler prokaryotic cells largely avoid. The cytoskeleton is the eukaryotic cell's solution to that challenge, providing both the structural framework and the transportation infrastructure needed to keep a large, compartmentalized cell functioning as an organized whole rather than a chaotic mixture of parts.
